title: Forest loss is slowing but land, commodity, conservation, and community-use pressures remain unevenly distributed
geography: 236 countries and areas, with forest extent, change, condition, management, ownership, use, disturbance, and carbon estimates for 1990-2025

observations.period: 1990-2025; global forest extent and net forest change

denominator.unit: countries and areas covered by FAO Global Forest Resources Assessment 2025

forest_area_2025.unit: hectares of global forest area in 2025, approximately

forest_land_share.unit: percent of global land area covered by forests

net_forest_loss_1990_2000.unit: hectares per year of annual net forest loss in 1990-2000

net_forest_loss_2015_2025.unit: hectares per year of annual net forest loss in 2015-2025

observations.method: FAO assessment based on official national data, remote sensing, country reporting, expert review, and standardized definitions across 236 countries and areas.
observations.uncertainty: National data quality, definitions, monitoring methods, and update timing differ; net forest-area change combines deforestation, forest expansion, and natural regeneration and is not identical to ecological condition or biodiversity.
observations.subgroup: Forest-dependent communities, Indigenous peoples, agricultural and commodity-producing regions, forest owners and managers, biodiversity, climate, water, and land-use systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Slower net loss is meaningful but does not mean forests are recovering everywhere; replacement forests, degraded forests, and plantations may not provide the same ecological or cultural functions as primary forests.

observations.period: 2015-2025; deforestation, forest expansion, and natural-regeneration pathways

denominator.unit: global forest-change and forest-type assessment frame

deforestation_rate_2015_2025.unit: hectares per year of deforestation in 2015-2025

forest_expansion_rate_2015_2025.unit: hectares per year of forest expansion in 2015-2025

naturally_regenerating_share.unit: percent of global forest area that is naturally regenerating

primary_forest_area.unit: hectares of primary forest, at least, representing about 29% of total forest area

observations.method: FAO comparison of deforestation, forest expansion, naturally regenerating forest, and primary-forest estimates across the 1990-2025 assessment period.
observations.uncertainty: Definitions of primary forest, natural regeneration, expansion, and deforestation are operational categories; area change does not by itself measure habitat quality, carbon permanence, local access, or cultural meaning.
observations.subgroup: Tropical and subtropical forest regions, agricultural frontiers, forest-dependent livelihoods, conservation institutions, restoration projects, and communities affected by land-use change.
observations.counterinterpretation: Expansion and restoration can improve landscape function and livelihoods when locally governed, but they cannot automatically substitute for intact primary forests or secure community rights.

observations.period: 2020-2025; forest ownership, management, protection, and social-use allocation

denominator.unit: global forest governance and management assessment frame

public_ownership.unit: percent of global forest area publicly owned as of 2020

private_ownership.unit: percent of global forest area privately owned as of 2020

protected_area_share.unit: approximately percent of global forest area in legally established protected areas in 2025

management_plan_share.unit: percent of global forest area covered by long-term management plans in 2025

social_services_objective.unit: percent of global forest area designated primarily for social services such as recreation, culture, and education

observations.method: FAO synthesis of forest ownership, legal protection, management-plan coverage, and primary management objectives.
observations.uncertainty: Formal ownership, protection, and management designation do not prove enforcement, local consent, benefit sharing, access, safety, or effective stewardship; social-service categories may undercount multifunctional use.
observations.subgroup: Public agencies, private owners, forest managers, Indigenous and local communities, recreation and cultural users, conservation organizations, and downstream water and climate beneficiaries.
observations.counterinterpretation: Formal plans and protected status can provide institutional leverage for conservation and public benefits, but outcomes depend on governance, financing, monitoring, and community rights.

related_sources.claim: FAO Global Forest Resources Assessment 2025 digital report record.
FAO forest carbon emissions and removals derived from FRA 2025.

boundary: This record adds a forest-land-use-to-livelihoods, commodity, public-ownership, conservation, cultural-use, and climate-capacity route. It is not local property or benefit-incidence data, does not establish household dependence or community consent, and does not equate forest area with ecological or social well-being.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official FAO FRA 2025 assessment page, interactive key-facts page, newsroom release, digital report record, and forest carbon release were retrieved; forest extent, net loss, deforestation, expansion, forest type, ownership, protection, management, and social-use claims were cross-checked.
